opus-5.5.text:
Yes, this is a problem that's easy to miss until you look closely. If you ask a modern text-to-image model for "a photo of a person," or even "a woman in her thirties smiling in a café," and generate a hundred samples, many of the faces start to look like siblings. The images are high quality and photorealistic, but they keep returning to a handful of facial prototypes. We think of it as a kind of mode collapse in identity space: the model has learned a very strong prior for what an attractive, well-lit, "typical" face looks like, and fine-tuning for aesthetics or preference tends to sharpen that prior even more.

With DISCO, the core idea is to treat facial diversity as something we explicitly measure and optimize for, rather than hoping it emerges from the training data. The first step is defining a good signal. We don't want diversity in pixel space, where a change in lighting or background counts as "different." We want diversity in identity, so we use face-recognition-style embeddings, which are designed to tell two people apart while ignoring pose, expression, and illumination. In that space, we can actually quantify how similar the generated faces are to one another for the same prompt.

The second step is using that signal to adjust the generator. Instead of rewarding each image independently, which is how most reward-based fine-tuning works, we look at groups of samples generated from the same prompt and reward the model when those samples are spread out in identity space. So the objective is defined over the set, not just the individual image. That matters, because a single image can't be "diverse" on its own. Diversity is a property of the distribution.

The third piece is not breaking anything else. If you push only for diversity, the model can cheat by producing distorted faces or ignoring the prompt. So we balance the diversity term with terms that preserve prompt fidelity and image quality, keeping the model close to its original behavior on everything except the tendency to collapse onto the same few faces. If the prompt specifies age, ethnicity, or a particular attribute, the model should still respect it. We want variety within the space the prompt allows, not random drift outside it.

What's nice about this framing is that it's fairly general. Faces are the most noticeable case, because humans are extremely sensitive to facial similarity, but the same set-level thinking applies to other kinds of homogenization in generative models. For faces specifically, the result is that you can generate a crowd scene or a batch of portraits and actually get distinct individuals, which matters for creative applications, for synthetic data generation, and frankly for representation, because the faces a model defaults to say a lot about whose faces it considers "normal."

r001.rationale: It contrasts high-quality, photorealistic faces with faces that look like siblings or reuse a handful of facial prototypes.

r002.rationale: It describes a strong learned prior and aesthetic or preference fine-tuning that sharpens it, then explains that ordinary reward-based fine-tuning rewards images independently rather than encouraging identity diversity.

r003.rationale: It describes reward-based adjustment and preserving the model's original behavior, but does not clearly identify reinforcement-learning fine-tuning of an existing text-to-image model as DISCO's approach.

r004.rationale: The diversity reward is described for groups of samples generated from the same prompt, not for distinct identities among people within one generated image.

r005.rationale: It explicitly rewards samples generated from the same prompt when they are spread out in identity space.

fable-5.1.text:
So the problem we started from is one that anybody who's played with these models has noticed. You ask for "a portrait of a woman" or "a man in a suit," and you get back what looks like the same handful of people over and over. The faces converge. The models have learned an average, and they sample from a very tight neighborhood around that average. And if you dig into it, you realize this isn't random. It's a consequence of how the training data is distributed, how the text embeddings collapse a vague prompt into basically one point in the conditioning space, and how classifier-free guidance pushes everything further toward the mode.

So with DISCO, which stands for diverse and inclusive sampling with compositional guidance, we tried to take that apart. The core observation is that a prompt like "a person" is underspecified, and the model fills in the missing attributes in a way that is heavily biased. Our thinking was: instead of leaving that to chance, let's make the latent attribute structure explicit and then steer the sampling process over it.

So there are really three pieces. First, we treat identity-relevant attributes, things like age, skin tone, facial structure, hair, as a compositional space, and we build guidance directions for each of them. These are not hand-drawn labels on individual images. We derive them from contrastive differences in the model's own representation, so we're not relying on some external face classifier that brings its own bias.

Second, during denoising, rather than just following one guidance vector toward "the prompt," we sample a trajectory through that attribute space. Early in the reverse process, when the coarse structure of the face is being decided, we inject diversity along those directions. Later, when fine detail is forming, we back off so we don't damage realism. That timing matters a lot. If you push too late, you get artifacts. If you push too early and too hard, you lose coherence with the text.

Third, and this is the part I think is most important, we do it as a population rather than one sample at a time. If a user asks for eight images, we want those eight to cover the space, not just be eight independent draws from the same mode. So we add a repulsion term across the batch, effectively a determinantal-style objective in the attribute space, so that samples push away from each other. Diversity becomes a property of the set, not just of each image.

And the thing we were careful about is that this has to be done without hurting prompt fidelity. If someone asks for "an elderly fisherman," we shouldn't start ignoring the "elderly" part in the name of diversity. So the guidance only operates on the attributes the prompt leaves open. We measure that, and we actually found that fidelity scores stay essentially flat while the identity diversity metrics go up substantially.

The broader point I'd make is that this isn't really about faces specifically. Faces are just where the collapse is most visible and most socially consequential. The same mode-seeking behavior shows up everywhere in these models. We just happened to attack it in the place where people notice it most.

r001.rationale: It contrasts preserving image realism with increasing identity diversity, conveying that realistic faces can still be insufficiently distinct.

r002.rationale: It blames repeated faces on data distribution, collapsed text embeddings, and classifier-free guidance, but does not say training objectives fail to explicitly encourage identity diversity.

r003.rationale: It describes attribute guidance during sampling, not reinforcement-learning fine-tuning of an existing model.

r004.rationale: Its diversity objective operates across a batch of separate images; it does not describe distinct identities within one generated image.

r005.rationale: It says a batch of images for a user's request should cover the attribute space, with samples repelling each other instead of repeating the same mode.

astra-6.text:
The key is to distinguish diversity from simply changing the random seed. You can generate different images—the background changes, the lighting changes—but the person still looks almost the same. So the question is, how do we get meaningful variation in identity while preserving what the text actually asks for?

With DISCO, the idea is to encourage that variation without losing alignment with the prompt. If you ask for a doctor, for example, the model should satisfy that description, but it shouldn’t treat “doctor” as specifying one particular face. There is a lot of freedom in the attributes you haven’t specified.

And those two things have to be evaluated together: are the faces genuinely different, and are the images still faithful to the description? Diversity by itself isn’t enough if you achieve it by ignoring the prompt.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts changing image details with changing identity, but does not distinguish realistic-looking faces from genuinely distinct identities.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute repeated identities to training objectives that fail to encourage identity diversity.

r003.rationale: It does not mention reinforcement-learning fine-tuning or an existing text-to-image model.

r004.rationale: It discusses variation across images, not distinct identities among people within a single generated image.

r005.rationale: It describes encouraging identity variation while preserving a prompt, but does not state that DISCO rewards diversity across separate generations using the same or similar prompts.

sol-6.1.text:
The issue is that a text prompt usually describes attributes, but it doesn’t specify a unique identity. If you ask for a person of a certain age with a certain hairstyle, there are many faces that could satisfy that description. Yet the model can keep returning a very similar, very typical face.

With DISCO, the idea is to encourage diversity while preserving the connection to the prompt. We want the model to explore different identities that all satisfy the description, rather than producing small variations of the same identity. Changing the background or the lighting isn’t enough—the faces themselves need to be meaningfully different.

So there are two things to balance: does each image still match what you asked for, and do the generated images actually cover different possibilities? Diversity is useful only if we maintain that semantic consistency.

r001.rationale: The response calls for meaningfully different identities, but it does not distinguish identity diversity from how realistic-looking the faces are.

r002.rationale: It attributes repeated faces to prompts that do not specify a unique identity, not to training objectives that fail to encourage identity diversity.

r003.rationale: It describes DISCO’s goal but does not identify reinforcement-learning fine-tuning of an existing model as its approach.

r004.rationale: It does not say DISCO rewards distinct identities among people within a single generated image.

r005.rationale: It discusses varied generated images satisfying one description, but does not clearly state that DISCO rewards identity diversity across separate generations using the same or similar prompts.
